summary: Describes a design for carrying IEEE 802.21 Media Independent Handover (MIH) messages across IP networks. It also covers how a mobile node can discover the mobility services it needs and how to transport the messages securely. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: When your phone moves from one kind of network to another, it needs helpers that tell it where to go. This document explains how the phone finds those helpers and talks to them over the Internet.

subtitle: How a mobile device finds the servers that help it switch networks, and how it talks to them over IP.

tldr.problem: IEEE 802.21 Media Independent Handover (MIH) helps a mobile node choose and switch networks, but it does not say how a node finds the server that offers these services or how MIH messages should cross an IP network.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC splits the problem in two. Discovery uses DNS or DHCP options to locate a Mobility Server, and transport carries MIH messages over TCP or UDP, with rules for message size, rate, retransmission and NAT.
tldr.outcome: It gives implementers a default transport (TCP, with UDP plus MIH acknowledgements for small event and command messages) and port 4551, but it defines no security. The IESG note urges careful analysis before any deployment.

facts.label: UDP rate if RTT unknown
facts.value: No more than one message every 3 seconds

today: RFC 5677 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It carries an IESG note that it provides no security mechanisms and that deployments need careful analysis. Discovery details are in RFC 5678 and RFC 5679.

sections.title: What the Framework Covers
sections.content:
IEEE 802.21 defines Media Independent Handover (MIH), a way to support handover of a device between different network types. Its services are the Information Service (IS), the Event Service (ES) and the Command Service (CS), together called Mobility Services (MoS). This RFC answers the problem statement in RFC 5164 about carrying MIH over layer 3, that is, over IP.

The work is divided in two parts. Discovery lets a mobile node (MN) learn the IP address of a node offering a service and which services it offers. Transport moves MIH messages between the MN and that node.

The RFC does not secure the MN to Mobility Server communication. It assumes link-layer or system-specific security, and it is RECOMMENDED against using the protocol without careful analysis of whether those mechanisms are good enough.
sections.eli5: A phone that moves around needs to find a helper and then talk to it. This document says how to find the helper and how to send messages to it.

sections.title: Where the Mobility Server Can Be
sections.content:
The relative position of the MN and the Mobility Server affects both discovery and signaling performance. The RFC lists four deployment scenarios.

  • S1, Home network MoS (MoSh): the MN and the services are both in the home network.
  • S2, Visited network MoS (MoSv): the MN is in a visited network and that network provides the services.
  • S3, Third-party MoS (MoS3): the services come from a network that is neither the home nor the current visited network.
  • S4, Roaming MoS: the MN is in a visited network but all services are provided by the home network.

Different types of service can be provided independently, and the entities providing them need not be co-located. IS tends to involve a large amount of static information, while ES and CS are dynamic and related: a handover command (CS) could follow a link event (ES). The document makes no assumption about where the services are.
sections.eli5: The helper might live in your home network, in the network you are visiting, in some third network, or back home while you travel. Your phone has to be able to find it in all four cases.

sections.title: Reference Model and Identifiers
sections.content:
On a node, the MIHF user sits on top. It is one or more MIH clients that generate queries and responses, process layer 2 triggers and carry out handover. Beneath it is the MIHF (Media Independent Handover Function), which does MoS discovery and creates, maintains, modifies and destroys MIH signaling associations with peer MIHFs. Under the MIHF are TCP and UDP for transport, and DHCP and DNS for finding peers.

Each MIHF endpoint has an MIHF identifier, which must be unique within the domain where services are provided and independent of the configured IP addresses. It MUST be written as an FQDN or as a Network Access Identifier (NAI). It can be pre-configured or discovered.

MIH messages need no extra framing because the MIH protocol already has a length field. Discovery MUST run when the MN gets no MoS information at attachment and has no pre-configured server, and the MN MUST refresh its MIHF peer bindings if its IP address changes.
sections.eli5: Inside the phone, a program asks for help, a middle part does the talking, and a bottom part sends the messages. Every helper has a name that stays the same even if its address changes.

sections.title: Discovering a Mobility Server
sections.content:
If the MN has a Mobility Server address pre-configured, no discovery is needed. Otherwise it uses one of two methods: DNS-based discovery from RFC 5679 or the DHCP options from RFC 5678. Which one fits depends on the scenario.

  • S1 (home): the MN SHOULD use DNS, and MUST have its home domain pre-configured. It MAY use the DHCP options instead.
  • S2 (visited): the MN SHOULD attempt the DHCP options.
  • S3 (third party): the MN MUST use DNS. It first has to learn the remote network's domain name, for example by sending an IS query to a Mobility Server it already knows.
  • S4 (home services while visiting): DNS applies, using the procedure for S1.

Authorization of an MN to use a specific Mobility Server is outside the scope of the RFC. If authorization is denied in future deployments, the MN should fall back to other learned servers.
sections.eli5: To find a helper, the phone either asks a directory (DNS) or asks the network that gave it its address (DHCP). Which one works best depends on where the helper is.

sections.title: Transporting MIH Messages
sections.content:
MIH peers MAY use TCP, UDP or any other transport both sides support. A Mobility Server MUST support both UDP and TCP and the MN MUST support TCP. TCP SHOULD be the default for all messages, but UDP combined with MIH acknowledgements SHOULD be used for ES and CS messages that fit within the path MTU. The MIH ACK mechanism MUST NOT be used with TCP because TCP already acknowledges and retransmits.

Size. MIH messages range from about 30 bytes (a capability discovery request) to around 65000 bytes (an IS response), while typical ES or CS messages are 50 to 100 bytes. With UDP, a limit MUST be set based on the path MTU, or the minimum MTU where PMTU is not implemented (the lesser of the first hop MTU and 576 bytes for IPv4 or 1280 bytes for IPv6). MIH-layer fragmentation MUST NOT be used together with IP fragmentation or over TCP.

Rate. If the RTT is unknown, a UDP sender SHOULD NOT average more than one message every 3 seconds, using a token bucket regulator.

Retransmission. Over UDP, MIH MUST use MIH ACKs. The default maximum number of retransmissions is 2, the initial timer (TMO) is 3 s when the RTT is not known, and the maximum TMO is 30 s.

NAT. TCP has no known NAT traversal issues. For UDP, MIH messages SHOULD be sent once every 2 minutes to refresh middlebox state, for example re-registration or event indication messages.

If no port is assigned (for example by DNS SRV), the default port from the IANA section MUST be used.
sections.eli5: Messages can go by a reliable but slower route (TCP) or a quick route with receipts (UDP). Big messages go the reliable way, and tiny urgent ones take the quick way.

sections.title: Example Operation Flow
sections.content:
The RFC walks through an IS request where the MN and the Mobility Server are in the MN's home network. DHCP is used for discovery and TCP carries the IS messages.

The MIH user sends a discovery request to the local MIHF. The MIHF invokes the DHCP client through an internal API, which sends a DHCP INFORM carrying the MoS option. The DHCP server answers with a DHCP ACK holding the Mobility Server address, and the MIHF returns a discovery response to the MIH user.

The MIH user then issues an IS query. The MIHF has a TCP client open a connection and sends the query in an MIH protocol REQUEST message. The Mobility Server MIHF hands it to its MIH user, and its answer returns in an MIH protocol RESPONSE message.
sections.eli5: The phone asks the network who the helper is and gets an address back. Then it calls the helper, asks a question and gets an answer.

sections.title: Security and the IESG Note
sections.content:
The IESG note says the specification provides no security mechanisms and deviates from the usual IETF requirement that security support is mandatory for Standards Track protocols. It recommends careful analysis before any deployment, and says this exception is not a precedent.

For discovery, administrators SHOULD use the DHCP authentication option from RFC 3118 where available or rely on link-layer security. Fake DNS requests and responses can cause denial of service or a failed handover, so DNS providers exposed to this are RECOMMENDED to use DNSSEC.

For transport, the listed threats are Mobility Server identity spoofing, tampering, replay attacks (the services support a push model) and eavesdropping that can reveal a user's movements. Link-layer security may suffice for the home and visited scenarios, but probably not for a third-party server. The RFC gives no deployment guidance beyond this.
sections.eli5: This document does not lock the doors. It warns that someone could trick the phone or spy on where it goes, so the network needs its own protection.
